listenings.text: Hi, this is Daniel from the Oliveira project. I just saw the new drawings and I have a question. The kitchen looks smaller than the one we agreed on last month. I am not angry, I just want to understand what happened before I show this to my wife. Could you call me back today and walk me through it? Thanks.

reading.rtitle: The email nobody wants to write
paras: Marina is an architect in Porto Alegre. Last Tuesday she opened her laptop and found a problem. The glass supplier for the Ribeiro house had just written to her: the special windows would arrive three weeks late.

She had two options. She could keep the original blueprint and accept a long delay, or she could change the layout of the back wall and use a different window. The second option was faster, but it meant a revision, and the client had already approved the first plan.

Marina did not send a long email. She called. She told the client what had happened, explained why she was suggesting the change, and said what it would cost: nothing extra, because the new windows were inside the same budget. She also said the deadline would move by four days, not three weeks.
The client asked two questions and then said yes. Later he told her that what he liked was not the solution. It was that she called before he had to ask.

gist.prompt: What is the main idea of the text?
choices: A supplier lost an important order and the project stopped.
An architect handled a problem by explaining the change early.
A client refused a revision because of the budget.

post_skill.title: Talk about it
items: Marina called instead of writing. Would you do the same? Why?
Have you ever had to tell a client or a boss about a delay? How did you start?
In your work, what is worse: a delay, or a change nobody explained?
The client said he liked being told before he had to ask. Why does that matter so much?

language_focus.title: These lines are from Marina's call. Match each one to what it does.
words: "We had to change the back wall."
"Instead of the special glass, we can use..."
"That way, we only lose four days."
"The good news is it stays inside the budget."
defs: shows the result of the new plan
protects the relationship with good news

language_focus.text: Notice the order Marina uses: what changed, why it changed, what you get instead, and what it costs. The order matters more than the words.

practice_a.title: Match each situation to the line that fits it best.
words: The client wants a bigger window, but the wall cannot take it.
The price of the wood went up.
The new plan finishes one week earlier.
defs: "That happened because of the market, not the project."
"We had to move the floor work to next week."
"That way, you get the keys before the holidays."
"Instead of one large window, we can use two smaller ones."

practice_a.text: Now pick ONE of the four and say the whole thing to your teacher: the change, the reason, and what the client gets. Add one sentence of your own.

practice_b.title: Reveal answer key
list: We had to make the kitchen a little smaller.
The delay happened because of the supplier.
Instead of marble, we can use a lighter stone.
That way, the work finishes sooner.
The good news is that the price did not change.
practice_b.note: Accept reasonable, justified variations; the key follows the student's output.

items: Situation
You are the architect. The client approved a plan last month. Today you found out the stone he chose is out of stock for six weeks. There is a similar stone, same price, available now.
Your task
Call the client. Announce the change, give the reason, offer the alternative, and say what it costs him. Your teacher plays the client and will ask at least two questions.

production.label: Useful language
items: We had to ...
That happened because of ...
Instead of ..., we can ...
That way, ...
The good news is ...
It will take about ...
Nothing changes on your side.

discussion.title: Discussion
items: Is it always better to call than to write? When is writing safer?
How much detail does a client really want about the reason?
In Brazil, do people expect an apology before an explanation? Does that change abroad?
Have you ever received bad news about a project well? What did the person do?
What is the hardest part for you: the bad news, or the English?
If the client gets angry anyway, what do you say next?

wrapup.title: Before you go
items: Which three words from today would you use in a real call tomorrow?
Say the four steps of a good explanation, in order.
One thing you want to practise more next class?
